title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Several Specific Opinions on How to Determine Whether Marital Affection Has Truly Broken Down in Divorce Cases Heard by People's Courts and the Several Opinions on the Handling of Cases of Cohabitation in the Name of Husband and Wife Without Marriage Registration by People's Courts
keywords_en: marriage; divorce; regarding the People's Court's adjudication of divorce cases; cohabitation under the name of husband and wife cases
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing Several Specific Opinions on How to Determine Whether the Marital Affection Has Truly Broken Down in Divorce Cases Tried by the People's Courts and Several Opinions on Cases of Cohabitation in the Name of Husband and Wife Without Marriage Registration

Fa (Min) Fa [1989] No. 38

To all local people's courts at various levels nationwide, all military courts at various levels, all railway transport intermediate courts and basic courts, and all maritime courts:

We are now issuing the "Several Specific Opinions on How to Determine Whether the Marital Affection Has Truly Broken Down in Divorce Cases Tried by the People's Courts" and the "Several Opinions on Cases of Cohabitation in the Name of Husband and Wife Without Marriage Registration". Please comply with and implement them, and pay attention to summarizing experience in the process of implementation. If you have any opinions or questions, please report them to this Court in a timely manner.

December 13, 1989

Several Specific Opinions on How to Determine Whether the Marital Affection Has Truly Broken Down in Divorce Cases Tried by the People's Courts

November 21, 1989

In trying divorce cases, the people's courts should take the true breakdown of marital affection as the criterion for distinguishing whether a divorce should be granted. To determine whether the marital affection has truly broken down, a comprehensive analysis should be conducted from aspects such as the foundation of the marriage, post-marital affection, reasons for divorce, the current state of the marital relationship, and the possibility of reconciliation. According to the relevant provisions of the Marriage Law and trial practice, if any of the following circumstances exists, marital affection shall be deemed to have truly broken down. If one party insists on divorce and mediation is ineffective, a divorce may be granted by judgment in accordance with the law.

1. One party suffers from a disease that is legally prohibited from marriage, or has a physical defect, or for other reasons cannot engage in sexual intercourse, and such condition is difficult to cure.

2. The parties lacked understanding before marriage, married hastily, and failed to establish marital affection after marriage, making it difficult to live together.

3. One party concealed a mental illness before marriage, which failed to be cured after treatment after marriage; or one party knew the other party suffered from a mental illness before marriage and still married him/her; or one party developed a mental illness during the common life of the husband and wife, which remained uncured after long-term treatment.

4. One party deceived the other party, or engaged in fraud during marriage registration to obtain a "Marriage Certificate".

5. After the parties completed marriage registration, they did not cohabit and have no possibility of reconciliation.

6. The marriage was arranged or bought and sold, and one party filed for divorce immediately after marriage, or even though the parties have lived together for many years, they have truly failed to establish marital affection.

7. The parties have been living apart due to affection disharmony for a full three years with truly no possibility of reconciliation; or, after the people's court rendered a judgment not granting divorce, the parties have lived apart for a full year and have mutually failed to fulfill marital obligations.

8. One party commits adultery or engages in illegal cohabitation with another person, and despite education, shows no signs of repentance; the party without fault initiates divorce proceedings; or the party at fault initiates divorce proceedings and the other party does not agree to divorce, and after criticism, education, disciplinary action, or after the people's court rendered a judgment not granting divorce, the party at fault again initiates divorce proceedings, and there is truly no possibility of reconciliation.

9. One party commits bigamy and the other party files for divorce.

10. One party is idle and fond of pleasure, has bad habits such as gambling, fails to fulfill family obligations, and refuses to change despite repeated admonitions, making it difficult for the parties to live together.

11. One party is legally sentenced to a long-term fixed-term imprisonment, or his/her illegal or criminal conduct seriously harms the marital affection.

12. One party has been missing for a full two years, and the other party files for divorce; after public notice and search, the whereabouts of the missing party are truly unknown.

13. One party is subjected to maltreatment or abandonment by the other party, or to maltreatment by the other party's relatives, or maltreats the other party's relatives, and after education, does not change, and the other party cannot forgive.

14. Other reasons lead to the true breakdown of marital affection.

Several Opinions on Cases of Cohabitation in the Name of Husband and Wife Without Marriage Registration

November 21, 1989

When trying cases of cohabitation in the name of husband and wife without marriage registration, the people's courts should first seriously point out to the parties the illegality and harmfulness of their conduct, and impose criticism and education or civil sanctions depending on the circumstances of the illegality. However, given the complexity of the reasons leading to such "marriage" relationships and the specific circumstances of the cases, in order to protect the legitimate rights and interests of women and children, facilitate the stability of marriage and family relationships, and maintain stability and unity, it is practical to conditionally recognize such de facto marital relationships within a certain period. To this end, based on legal provisions and trial practice, we propose the following opinions for trying such cases:

1. If, before the implementation of the "Marriage Registration Measures" on March 15, 1986, the parties cohabited in the name of husband and wife without completing marriage registration procedures, and the public also considered them to be husband and wife, and one party files a "divorce" lawsuit with the people's court, if both parties met the statutory conditions for marriage at the time of filing the lawsuit, the relationship may be recognized as a de facto marital relationship; if one or both parties did not meet the statutory conditions for marriage at the time of filing the lawsuit, the relationship shall be deemed as an illegal cohabitation relationship.

2. If, after the implementation of the "Marriage Registration Measures" on March 15, 1986, the parties cohabited in the name of husband and wife without completing marriage registration procedures, and the public also considered them to be husband and wife, and one party files a "divorce" lawsuit with the people's court, if both parties met the statutory conditions for marriage at the time of cohabitation, the relationship may be recognized as a de facto marital relationship; if one or both parties did not meet the statutory conditions for marriage at the time of cohabitation, the relationship shall be deemed as an illegal cohabitation relationship.

3. From the date of implementation of the new marriage registration administrative regulations of the Ministry of Civil Affairs, cohabitation in the name of husband and wife without marriage registration shall be treated as an illegal cohabitation relationship.

4. If, after divorce, both parties have not remarried and, without going through remarriage registration procedures, again live together in the name of husband and wife, and one party files a "divorce" lawsuit, generally the illegal cohabitation relationship should be dissolved.

5. If a party who has already registered a marriage forms a de facto marital relationship with a third party; or a party in a de facto marital relationship registers a marriage with a third party; or a party in a de facto marital relationship forms a new de facto marital relationship with a third party; if a party in the previous marital relationship demands that the bigamy be pursued, regardless of whether the act constitutes bigamy, the subsequent marital relationship should be dissolved. If a party in the previous marital relationship requests to handle the divorce issue, mediation or a judgment should be made in accordance with the specific circumstances of that marital relationship.

6. In trying divorce cases involving de facto marital relationships, mediation shall be conducted first. If mediation leads to reconciliation or withdrawal of the lawsuit, the marital relationship shall be confirmed as valid, and a mediation document or ruling document shall be issued; if mediation cannot achieve reconciliation, a divorce shall be granted by mediation or judgment.

7. If a man and a woman cohabiting in the name of husband and wife without marriage registration, and one party requests "divorce" or dissolution of the cohabitation relationship, and upon investigation it is indeed an illegal cohabitation relationship, a judgment shall be made uniformly to dissolve the relationship.

8. When trying cases involving illegal cohabitation relationships, if issues such as the custody of non-marital children and the division of property are involved, these shall be resolved together. When specifically dividing property, the interests of women and children shall be taken into account, the actual circumstances of the property and the degree of fault of the parties shall be considered, and a proper division shall be made.

9. When dissolving an illegal cohabitation relationship, the custody of the non-marital children born to the parties shall be determined by agreement between the parties; if agreement cannot be reached, a judgment shall be made based on the interests of the children and the specific circumstances of the parties. For children who are still being breastfed, in principle, the mother shall have custody; however, if the father's conditions are good and the mother agrees, the father may also have custody. For children who are persons with limited capacity for civil conduct, the children's own opinions shall be sought. If one party intends to place a minor child for adoption by another person, the consent of the other party must be obtained.

10. When dissolving an illegal cohabitation relationship, the income jointly obtained by both parties during the cohabitation period and the property jointly purchased during that period shall be treated as co-owned property. Property voluntarily given by one party to the other party before cohabitation may be handled by analogy with a gift relationship; property obtained by one party from the other party through demand may be handled with reference to the spirit of Article (18) of the Supreme People's Court's "Several Opinions on Implementing Civil Policy and Legal Issues" (Fa Ban Fa [1984] No. 112).

11. When dissolving an illegal cohabitation relationship, claims and debts arising from joint production and livelihood during the cohabitation period may be treated as joint claims and debts.

12. When dissolving an illegal cohabitation relationship, if one party suffers from a serious illness that remains uncured during the period of common life, appropriate consideration shall be given when dividing property, or the other party may provide one-time financial assistance.

13. If one party dies during the cohabitation period and the other party claims inheritance of the deceased's estate, if the relationship is recognized as a de facto marital relationship, the matter may be handled in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Inheritance Law in the capacity of a spouse; if the relationship is recognized as an illegal cohabitation relationship but meets the conditions provided in Article 14 of the Inheritance Law, the matter may be handled based on the specific circumstances of mutual support.

14. When trying cases of cohabitation in the name of husband and wife without marriage registration, if the illegal conduct is serious, appropriate civil sanctions shall be imposed in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Marriage Law, the General Principles of the Civil Law, the "Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law", and other laws and regulations.

15. These Opinions shall come into effect on the date of promulgation. Where any previous provisions of the Supreme People's Court conflict with these Opinions, these Opinions shall prevail.
